Rudolf Kassner’s comments from April 1942 in the Europäische Revue seem extraordinarily illuminating.
Hobbes is the true philosopher of the Baroque.
The Baroque puts up a façade in front of the new, Faustian world and makes that façade swell with importance. There is a separation between rule and power:
Hobbes’s separation between outside and inside, with the strongest possible emphasis on the outside, does indeed have something of this putting-forward of the façade.
“Desire of power, that ceaseth only in death.”
Even Leviathan is a mortal god, a Deus mortalis.
Kassner is entirely right when he says:

“Hobbes’s view of power is neither that of the Greek Sophists, nor that of Machiavelli, nor that of Goethe’s Mephistopheles. None of them, when thinking of power, thinks of either death or sin; they remain in the real (? sic!).”
With this “ceaseth in death,” something loosens in the connection between being and power.
Hobbes does not recoil from death in horror. But he sees it. He seeks protection in power—but only protection from death at the hands of other human beings.
Power must not be allowed to kill on its own authority. That is the decisive point.
Poor metabolists that we are—poor creatures of change!

Life is the façade in front of death.

Prestige, glory, honour, representation, omnipotence—but still, in the end, an external omnipotence.
Back then, in the Baroque age, the superiority of the inner over the outer was not yet taken for granted as it is today.
The whole psychology and sociology of “unmasking” was a dismantling of the Baroque façade in order to expose the naked core of power beneath it.
Republic = verta = laying bare of force (virtus).

Behind it lies the need for security among competing powers and, ultimately, among competing individuals.
For the individual, precisely because he is an individual, is forced to set himself down, distinguish himself from others, assert himself, and practise a politics of power.
Strangely, Behemoth is not as suitable a façade as Leviathan.
